subject: chemistry
title: Transition metals as catalysts
key_idea: Transition metals are good catalysts because they have several stable oxidation states and vacant d orbitals that bond to reactants. A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase and works on its surface. A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase and works through an intermediate.

sections.heading: Why transition metals are good catalysts

blocks.text: Two features of transition metals explain their catalytic activity.

items: **More than one stable oxidation state:** the metal can gain and lose electrons, so it can be oxidised and reduced during the reaction and then return to its original state.
**Vacant, accessible d orbitals:** they form dative bonds with ligands, so reactant molecules can bind to the metal.
Bonding to the surface or metal ion holds reactants close together and weakens their bonds. This gives a reaction path with a lower activation energy.

items.meaning: A catalyst in a different phase from the reactants. The reaction happens at active sites on its surface.
A catalyst in the same phase as the reactants. The reaction goes through an intermediate species.

items: Variable oxidation states let the catalyst be used up and reformed.
Vacant d orbitals let reactants bond to the catalyst.
Heterogeneous: different phase. Homogeneous: same phase.

blocks.text: A solid catalyst works on gas or liquid reactants by four steps at its surface.

diagram.alt: Put the stages of heterogeneous catalysis in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the stages of heterogeneous catalysis in order.
steps: Reactant molecules are adsorbed onto active sites on the surface
Bonds in the reactants are weakened
The reactants react on the surface
Product molecules are desorbed from the surface

items: In a catalytic converter, CO and NO are adsorbed, the bonds weaken, and they react. CO₂ and N₂ are desorbed.
The catalyst is spread thinly on a **support medium**, such as a ceramic honeycomb. This maximises the surface area and uses less of the costly metal.
Catalysts can be **poisoned** by impurities that bind to the active sites and block them, for example sulfur compounds with iron. The catalyst works less well.
Poisoning has a cost: the feed must be purified, or the catalyst replaced or regenerated.

items.text: SO₂ + V₂O₅ → SO₃ + V₂O₄. Vanadium goes from +5 to +4.
2V₂O₄ + O₂ → 2V₂O₅. Vanadium goes back from +4 to +5.

blocks.text: The catalyst is unchanged overall. Its change of oxidation state is what allows it to catalyse.

items: Adsorption, bond weakening, reaction, desorption.
A support increases surface area and cuts cost; poisons block active sites.
V₂O₅ is reduced to V₂O₄ and then reoxidised to V₂O₅.

blocks.text: A homogeneous catalyst is used in one step and reformed in a later step. The reaction has an intermediate.

blocks.label: Overall reaction
where: Slow uncatalysed: two negative ions repel each other.

blocks.text: Each step is between a positive and a negative ion, so there is no repulsion and the activation energy is lower. Fe³⁺ can start the cycle instead.

blocks.label: Overall reaction
where: Mn²⁺ is a product and also the catalyst. This is autocatalysis.

diagram.alt: The concentration of Mn²⁺ rises slowly at first, then quickly as the catalyst builds up, then levels off when the reactants are used up.

items: At first the reaction is slow, because MnO₄⁻ and C₂O₄²⁻ are both negative ions and repel.
Mn²⁺ forms and reacts with MnO₄⁻ to give Mn³⁺, which then reacts with C₂O₄²⁻ and reforms Mn²⁺.
The rate increases as more catalyst forms, then falls as reactants run out.
Homogeneous catalysts work through an intermediate, using their variable oxidation state.
Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ alternate in the I⁻ and S₂O₈²⁻ reaction.
Mn²⁺ autocatalyses its own formation, so the reaction speeds up.

checks.q: Explain why transition metals are good catalysts.
checks.a: They have more than one stable oxidation state, so can be oxidised and reduced and then reformed. They have vacant d orbitals that can form dative bonds with reactants.

checks.q: Explain, with equations, how V₂O₅ catalyses the oxidation of SO₂ in the Contact process.
checks.a: SO₂ + V₂O₅ → SO₃ + V₂O₄ (V is reduced from +5 to +4). 2V₂O₄ + O₂ → 2V₂O₅ (V is oxidised back from +4 to +5).

checks.q: Explain why the reaction between MnO₄⁻ and C₂O₄²⁻ starts slowly and then speeds up.
checks.a: Both ions are negative and repel, so the uncatalysed reaction is slow. The Mn²⁺ ions formed act as a catalyst (autocatalysis), so the rate increases.

items: Practical examples of catalytic behaviour: Cu²⁺ in the reaction of zinc with acids, and MnO₂ in the decomposition of H₂O₂.
Transition metal catalysts matter in industry: iron for ammonia and V₂O₅ for sulfuric acid.

A catalytic converter decreases CO and NO emissions from internal combustion engines by adsorption of CO and NO onto the catalyst surface, weakening of bonds and reaction, and desorption of CO₂ and N₂.
V₂O₅ acts as a catalyst in the Contact process, explained in terms of oxidation number.
Know the role of Fe²⁺ in catalysing the I⁻ and S₂O₈²⁻ reaction, and of Mn²⁺ in autocatalysing the MnO₄⁻ and C₂O₄²⁻ reaction.
Use equations to explain the catalysis by V₂O₅, by Fe²⁺ (I⁻ and S₂O₈²⁻) and by Mn²⁺ (C₂O₄²⁻ and MnO₄⁻).
Explain the importance of variable oxidation states in catalysis.
Fe is the heterogeneous catalyst in the Haber process.
Poisoning of a heterogeneous catalyst reduces its efficiency and has a cost implication.

Heterogeneous mode of action: adsorption of reactants, bond weakening and desorption of products. Examples: iron in the Haber process; palladium, platinum and rhodium removing oxides of nitrogen from car exhausts.
Homogeneous catalysts are used in one step and reformed in a later step. Examples: atmospheric oxides of nitrogen in the oxidation of atmospheric SO₂, and Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺ in the I⁻ and S₂O₈²⁻ reaction.
Nitrogen oxides example: 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, then NO₂ + SO₂ → NO + SO₃. NO is reformed.
